strengths: The manuscript studies a relevant problem and presents an intuitive approach: formulate audio inpainting as masked-token generation using WavTokenizer and a discrete diffusion transformer.
Operating in compressed token space is computationally attractive, and waveform splicing with a short crossfade is a practical way to preserve uncorrupted audio.

The evaluation in the source manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/d0bb3a703c60467fb174b03aab4264f2/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} covers several gap lengths and reports complementary distributional, spectral, and perceptual metrics.
weaknesses: The main novelty is limited: the method primarily combines an existing tokenizer, an existing discrete-diffusion objective, and a standard DiT, without a new architectural or learning contribution specific to audio inpainting.
The central 500 ms and MTG-dataset claims in the abstract and conclusion are unsupported: the experimental section reports only MusicNet results for gaps up to 300 ms.

The comparison is not sufficiently controlled or documented. Baseline values appear to be taken from prior work, but the paper does not establish identical test clips, preprocessing, metric implementations, or statistical comparability. No confidence intervals, repeated runs, or significance tests are reported.

The evaluation uses only 60 clips from one musical dataset and lacks subjective listening tests. Whole-clip reference metrics may be dominated by the unchanged context, while gap-only quality, boundary artifacts, temporal coherence, and sample diversity are not evaluated.

Essential ablations are absent, including comparisons with masked-token prediction without diffusion, alternative tokenizers or continuous latent models, tokenizer reconstruction as an oracle, and the effects of diffusion steps, crossfading, and context length.

Reproducibility is poor: the DiT depth, width, parameter count, tokenizer checkpoint and configuration, sampling rate, masking distribution, noise schedule, reverse solver, number of inference steps, and metric implementation details are missing. The promised audio-example link is also blank, and no code or models are provided.

Claims that token-space diffusion improves stability, long-range coherence, oversmoothing, or spectral blurring are asserted rather than directly measured. Given the incremental contribution and substantial evidential gaps, the paper is not yet competitive for a top-tier AI conference.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: restoring relatively long gaps in musical audio.
Representing audio with WavTokenizer tokens and performing absorbing-state discrete diffusion is intuitive and potentially computationally attractive.
The high-level pipeline is easy to understand, and the evaluation considers several complementary objective metrics and multiple gap lengths.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are not supported. The abstract claims evaluation on MTG through 500 ms, and the conclusion claims strong performance at 500 ms, but the experiments contain only MusicNet results through 300 ms.

The baseline evaluation is inadequate. Baselines appear only in a plot, without numerical results, uncertainty estimates, significance tests, or a clear statement that they were rerun on exactly the same examples and preprocessing. Comparing the proposed FAD to an approximate value reported by prior work does not establish a controlled improvement.

The evaluation is very small—60 short MusicNet excerpts—and lacks subjective listening tests despite making claims about perceptual quality, semantic coherence, realism, and listening experience. The reported ODG values near -3 also indicate substantial perceptual impairment.

Essential implementation details are absent, including transformer depth, width, attention configuration, parameter count, diffusion schedule, number of sampling steps, tokenizer checkpoint and token rate, masking distribution, gap-to-token alignment, and inference settings. Reproduction is therefore not feasible.

There are no ablations isolating the benefits of discrete diffusion, the pretrained tokenizer, crossfading, context conditioning, or model scale. A tokenizer-only oracle/reconstruction bound and comparisons against masked-token or autoregressive token models are also missing.

The technical contribution is limited: the method largely combines a pretrained WavTokenizer with an existing discrete-diffusion objective and a standard diffusion transformer, without a new algorithmic component tailored to audio inpainting.

Metric computation is underspecified. In particular, the FAD embedding variant and aggregation protocol are unclear, and it is not stated whether metrics cover only missing regions or complete clips. This is important because most samples remain uncorrupted and can dominate full-clip scores.

Several inconsistencies further reduce confidence: the paper alternates between gaps starting at 25 and 50 ms, provides no 500 ms results, claims to outperform CQT-Diff+ across all metrics without a complete numeric table, and leaves the promised audio-example URL blank.

The presentation contains numerous typographical and grammatical errors, including the misspelled title, and the method section is too cursory for a top-tier technical paper. Overall, unsupported headline claims and an insufficiently controlled evaluation constitute fundamental deficiencies rather than minor omissions.

strengths: The paper explores a sensible and potentially useful direction: formulating music inpainting as discrete token completion using a pretrained WavTokenizer and an absorbing-state discrete diffusion model.

The token-space approach can substantially shorten sequences relative to waveform modeling and may provide a practical computational advantage; the reported training requirement of one A6000 GPU for two days is encouraging.
The method is conceptually straightforward, and preserving the original waveform outside the gap with a short boundary crossfade is a pragmatic design choice.
The MusicNet results suggest promising FAD performance, especially for longer gaps: the reported FAD of 3.81 at 300 ms is better than the plotted CQT-Diff+ result.
The paper evaluates several complementary objective metrics and considers multiple gap durations.
weaknesses: The central experimental claims are not adequately supported. The abstract and conclusion claim evaluation on MTG and strong performance for 500 ms gaps, but the paper presents no MTG setup, 500 ms results, table, figure, or analysis.

The assertion that AIDD outperforms CQT-Diff+ across all metrics contradicts Figure 3. AIDD appears competitive on LSD and FAD, but its ODG is markedly worse than CQT-Diff+ and several other baselines. This discrepancy undermines the conclusions.

The evaluation is too limited for a top-tier paper: it uses only 60 MusicNet excerpts, has no confidence intervals or statistical tests, and provides no listening study despite emphasizing perceptual plausibility and semantic coherence. Metrics such as FAD alone cannot establish whether an inpainted passage is contextually or musically coherent.

Baseline methodology is insufficiently documented. It is unclear whether baselines were rerun on exactly the same samples and preprocessing or whether values were transcribed from prior work. There is no comparison with important learned long-gap methods such as MAID or GACELA, and no tokenizer-based non-diffusion baseline.

There are no ablations isolating the effects of discrete diffusion, WavTokenizer, the crossfade, context length, diffusion steps, or token corruption schedule. Consequently, the results do not show whether any advantage comes from the proposed generative model rather than the codec or postprocessing.

The method is not specified well enough for reproduction. Missing details include Transformer depth and width, parameter count, attention configuration, vocabulary size and tokenizer checkpoint, noise schedule, sampling algorithm and number of reverse steps, gap-to-token alignment, conditioning/masking procedure, and metric implementation details.

The novelty is currently modest: the method largely combines an existing pretrained audio tokenizer with an existing discrete diffusion objective and a standard Diffusion Transformer, without a clearly developed inpainting-specific technical contribution.

The evaluation may be affected by codec receptive fields and boundary leakage: the manuscript says that a waveform containing a silent gap is encoded, but does not explain how corrupted waveform intervals map to masked token positions or whether surrounding tokens can encode information from the target region. The 10 ms crossfade also needs to be applied consistently to baselines for a fair comparison.

The paper lacks basic completeness and polish: the promised audio-example link is empty, code and checkpoints are not provided, and numerous typographical and grammatical errors remain. These issues are especially consequential for an audio-generation paper whose qualitative outputs cannot otherwise be assessed.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and challenging problem: musically coherent reconstruction of relatively long audio gaps.
Representing audio with WavTokenizer tokens makes long-context modeling more computationally tractable, and applying discrete diffusion to music inpainting is a potentially useful direction.
Experiments cover two datasets and several gap durations, with encouraging reported improvements over classical, GAN-based, and continuous-diffusion baselines.
The ablation table examines span corruption, first- and second-order derivative losses, and several hyperparameter settings.
weaknesses: The method is technically underspecified. The model predicts categorical score ratios, but the derivative loss is defined on a “predicted embedding” without explaining how that embedding is obtained differentiably from the categorical predictions, which embedding space is used, or how masked-neighbor cases are handled.

Span masking introduces dependencies between token positions, whereas the presented DWDSE objective and reverse process are derived for the stated token-level transition process. The paper does not define the resulting joint forward process or justify that the same objective and reverse sampler remain valid.

The inference procedure is ambiguous: encoding a waveform containing silence does not itself produce mask tokens. The paper does not precisely explain how gap locations are mapped to tokens, how affected tokens are initialized and clamped during reverse diffusion, or provide the noise schedule, sampling steps, and boundary-token treatment.

The evaluation is too limited to establish perceptual superiority. MusicNet uses only 60 excerpts, MAESTRO reports only one objective metric, and there is no human listening study despite long-gap completion being inherently multimodal and reference-based metrics being unreliable for plausible alternatives.

Baseline comparability is unclear. The MAESTRO subset and test examples are unspecified, prior methods apparently used the full dataset, and it is not stated clearly whether every baseline was rerun on identical examples and metric implementations. Consequently, the state-of-the-art comparisons are difficult to validate.

The ablation is confounded because the base model is reportedly trained for 400k steps while other variants are trained for 100k steps. Moreover, the combined method is not consistently best: derivative-only or span-only variants outperform it on several 300 ms metrics, contradicting the paper's summary.

Important reproducibility information is missing, including model depth/width/head count and parameter count, tokenizer checkpoint and audio preprocessing, MAESTRO subset identities, masking overlap and budget handling, diffusion schedule, and inference configuration. The listed “sampling rate” of 128 is also unexplained and appears inconsistent with the audio/token rates described.

There is no tokenizer reconstruction control or oracle experiment, making it impossible to separate diffusion performance from codec effects. Claims about semantic coherence, stability, efficiency, and model-size/training-time advantages are also not directly measured or sufficiently documented.

The proposed components have limited demonstrated novelty beyond combining an existing tokenizer and discrete-diffusion framework; span masking is a common sequence-modeling strategy, while smoothness in an arbitrary token-embedding space is not shown to correspond to waveform or perceptual smoothness.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and challenging problem—music inpainting over relatively long gaps—and the use of discrete audio tokens is a plausible way to reduce sequence length and capture higher-level structure.

The proposed system is evaluated on two established music datasets and against several classical, GAN-based, and diffusion-based methods. The reported results are promising, especially on MusicNet for 200–300 ms gaps and on MAESTRO according to ODG.
The paper includes component ablations covering span masking, derivative order, and several hyperparameter settings.
The overall pipeline and motivation are understandable, and the inference-time crossfade is a sensible practical detail.
weaknesses: The span-corruption process is not adequately reconciled with the discrete-diffusion theory used to justify the DWDSE objective. Exact-budget, correlated span masking does not obviously follow the stated token-independent absorbing continuous-time Markov process. The paper neither derives the corresponding transition probabilities/reverse process nor establishes that the original DWDSE objective remains valid under this modification.

The derivative loss is underspecified. The model predicts categorical scores, but the paper does not explain how a differentiable predicted embedding is obtained from these scores. More fundamentally, temporal proximity or smoothness in a learned codec's codebook embedding space is not shown to correspond to waveform or perceptual continuity.

The central claim that the combined method is consistently best is contradicted by Table 3. At 300 ms, derivative-only training has better FAD than the reported combined model, while span-only training matches or improves several LSD/ODG results. Many differences are also smaller than the reported variability, with no significance analysis.

The evaluation is too limited for strong perceptual or state-of-the-art claims. MusicNet uses only 60 excerpts, MAESTRO uses an unspecified random subset, and there is no human listening study despite semantic coherence and perceptual naturalness being central claims. FAD is particularly questionable on such a small evaluation collection.

The MAESTRO comparison does not establish a controlled experiment. The manuscript suggests prior systems used the full dataset while AIDD used an undisclosed subset, but it does not clearly state that all methods were rerun on exactly the same test excerpts and preprocessing. Consequently, the numerical comparison may conflate model quality with differing evaluation sets or implementations.

Important controls are missing, including codec reconstruction and oracle-token ceilings, a conventional masked-token Transformer, independent masking under the same architecture and training budget, and comparisons with more directly relevant conditional audio-inpainting systems. These omissions prevent attribution of gains to discrete diffusion, span masking, or the pretrained tokenizer.

Hyperparameter selection appears to use the reported test protocol: numerous variants are compared on MusicNet, yet no validation split or selection procedure is described. This creates a substantial risk of test-set tuning.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The architecture size and depth, tokenizer checkpoint and audio sample rate, diffusion/noise schedule, number of sampling steps, conditioning mechanism, span-overlap handling, gap-to-token alignment, and exact dataset subsets are omitted. Table 4's 'sampling rate 128' is unexplained and appears erroneous. Statements about model size and training efficiency are unsupported by complete measurements.

Training budgets are inconsistent: the base MusicNet model is trained for 400k steps while other variants use 100k, and the supplementary description is not fully consistent with the main text. Runtime, inference cost, parameter counts, and matched-compute comparisons are absent.

The novelty is incremental without stronger validation: the method primarily combines a pretrained tokenizer, an existing discrete-diffusion objective, span masking, and an embedding-space smoothness penalty. Given the theoretical gaps and weak experimental controls, the evidence does not meet the standard for acceptance at a top-tier AI conference.

strengths: The paper explores a relevant and under-studied direction: performing music inpainting through discrete diffusion over compact audio tokens. Combining WavTokenizer with a diffusion transformer is intuitive and potentially useful for long gaps.
The empirical results are promising. AIDD improves most MusicNet metrics at 200–300 ms and reports the best MAESTRO ODG at 375 and 750 ms, despite comparatively modest stated compute.
Evaluation spans two datasets, several gap lengths, and classical, sparse, GAN-based, and diffusion-based baselines.

The ablation table examines span masking, first- and second-order derivative losses, and several hyperparameter settings. The method is also computationally attractive if the claimed model-size and training-time advantages hold.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not yet convincingly establish the perceptual claims. There is no human listening study, and the promised audio-example link is absent. This is important because objective metrics can correlate poorly with the semantic and musical coherence emphasized by the paper.

The reported gains lack statistical support. MusicNet uses only 60 excerpts, FAD is reported without uncertainty, and no significance testing is provided. On MAESTRO, the 750 ms improvement over bin2bin-MIDI is only 0.017, far smaller than the reported variability.

The ablation results do not support the assertion that the combined method is consistently best. At 300 ms, a derivative-only variant has better FAD, while a span-only variant has better LSD; span-only also matches or slightly exceeds combined ODG. Thus, the benefit of combining both proposed components is unclear.

Important methodological details are missing: transformer size and configuration, diffusion schedule and number of reverse steps, WavTokenizer checkpoint, construction of predicted embeddings for the derivative loss, masking of known context during reverse diffusion, and the exact FAD aggregation procedure. The appendix's “sampling rate 128” is ambiguous.

There is a theoretical mismatch that needs clarification. The DWDSE formulation and reverse transition in the paper assume token-wise transitions, whereas span corruption creates correlated transitions across positions. The manuscript does not derive a compatible objective/reverse process or explain why the original estimator remains valid.

Baseline comparability is insufficiently documented. It is unclear which baselines were rerun versus copied from prior work, whether preprocessing and test excerpts were identical, and how metric implementations were harmonized. The two datasets also use different ODG implementations.

The MAESTRO subset is unspecified and reportedly selected randomly, preventing exact reproduction and making the comparison with methods trained on the full dataset difficult to interpret. The manuscript also gives conflicting training descriptions: the main text states that the base MusicNet model used 400k steps, whereas the supplement says the highest reported model used 100k steps.

Claims about stability, long-range semantic coherence, generalization, model-size efficiency, and state-of-the-art performance are stronger than the evidence. No stability analysis, semantic metric, compute table, parameter count, tokenizer reconstruction control, or possible tokenizer-pretraining overlap analysis is provided. Overall, the idea and preliminary results are encouraging, but the technical specification and evaluation need substantial strengthening for a top-tier acceptance.
